transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-06-02 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 45 minutes (scheduled)
- Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Rachel Kim (Lyra - Head of ML), Ajay Patel (Lyra - Cloud Infra), Sofia Martinez (Lyra - CTO)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on unit economics — per-token pricing, batching and cache levers, and tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private deployment. Customer wants a concrete TCO example and a short dedicated trial to validate latency and cost.

Topics: pricing per token, batching/caching, quantization options, dedicated pool sizing, security/KMS, trial/benchmarks, timeline/budget constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro—I'm Liam, AE on the account, and Priya's our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Rachel (Lyra): Good, thanks. we've got about 45, so we want to focus on cost per inference and how that scales, tradeoffs with latency, and also security implications.
[00:22] Priya (Redwood): Awesome. we'll frame this around three modes—hosted API for fastest onboarding, dedicated for predictable throughput, and private for on-prem / VPC. then dive into per-token economics and batching/caching levers. sound good?
[00:32] Sofia (Lyra): Yes. high level first—what do you usually see for per-token cost and what's variable?
[00:40] Liam (Redwood): Great question. baseline hosted pricing is per-token with volume tiers. but the big levers to hit unit cost are batching, prefix / KV cache reuse, and quantization. basically you can trade a bit of latency for much lower per-token costs with batching and cache hits.
[00:56] Ajay (Lyra): when you say KV cache, is that the same as the K-V cash we've seen? sorry, transcription
[01:02] Priya (Redwood): haha yes, KV cache — key-value cache for decoder states; it reduces compute on repeated prefixes. for example, a chat with repeated system prompts or long context, you get cache hits that avoid recomputing tokens.
[01:20] Rachel (Lyra): can you quantify? like if we move from hosted to dedicated, and enable batching + cache, what kind of unit delta do we see?
[01:28] Priya (Redwood): ballpark: hosted might be 0.5-1.5x baseline per-token because of multi-tenant overhead and egress; dedicated can reduce that to maybe 0.6x-0.8x for similar model size when you tune batching. with aggressive batching and prefix caching, some workloads see 2-4x token cost improvements versus naive single-request mode. but it's workload dependent — short chat turns vs long-document generation differ.
[01:55] Sofia (Lyra): that's a pretty wide range. our workload is mainly short responses (avg 30 tokens) but high QPS during market opens. we care a lot about p50 latency <= 150ms and p95 under 500ms.
[02:10] Liam (Redwood): right. short-turn, low-latency workloads are trickier to batch. for those, dedicated + smaller batch windows and prefix caching help, but batching benefit is lower. we usually recommend a mix: keep a hosted fallback for burstiness and a dedicated pool for steady steady baseline.
[02:30] Ajay (Lyra): what about quantization? can that be used in hosted? or is that only on dedicated/private?
[02:36] Priya (Redwood): hosted supports verified quantized model variants we curate, but dedicated/private gives you more control—custom quant profiles and more aggressive int8/int4 options. note: aggressive quant can slightly impact quality; we pair quant recommendations with eval suites to ensure no regressions.
[02:54] Rachel (Lyra): budget-wise, we have a nightly batch job for document summarization and realtime chat for traders. nightly batch is flexible on latency, chat isn't. what's a simple example TCO to compare?
[03:05] Liam (Redwood): we can do a worked example — say you have 1M short-chat tokens/day and 10M batch tokens overnight. hosted per-token price x gives you Y; dedicated fixed monthly plus reserved capacity amortized across tokens yields lower per-token for the batch, and similar or slightly better for chat depending on batch windows. we'll send a pricing worksheet with numbers.
[03:28] Sofia (Lyra): can you share a sample calc on the call?
[03:31] Liam (Redwood): we didn't prep exact numbers for you but we'll follow up with the sheet — Liam will send it.
[03:36] Priya (Redwood): in practice, the levers we tune for Lyra's profile are: smaller batch windows for chat, aggressive KV caching for repeated prompts (market opens use-case), and quantization on batch pipeline. also consider model routing—cheap model for low-value summarization, higher quality for chat.
[03:55] Ajay (Lyra): model routing—do you support automatic fallback if dedicated pool is saturated?
[03:59] Priya (Redwood): yes, smart routing: policy-based. you can route by latency SLO or cost; fallback to hosted or lower-cost model variant if capacity is constrained. that gives resilience during spikes.
[04:12] Rachel (Lyra): security — we need KMS, SSO, SOC2, and audit logs for compliance. which modes cover that?
[04:20] Liam (Redwood): Private (VPC/on-prem) and Dedicated (with Private control plane) both support KMS/HSM integrations, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs. hosted meets SOC2 and we can surface audit data, but some regulated customers prefer private for full network isolation. we'll attach our SOC2 and security packet.
[04:36] Sofia (Lyra): great. about the trial — you mentioned a dedicated trial pool. what's typical sizing?
[04:42] Priya (Redwood): depends on sustained QPS. for your short-chat avg 30 tokens and peak QPS numbers you'll provide, we'd size a small dedicated pool (1-2 GPUs equivalent) initially for 2 weeks, run synthetic and replay tests. that should illustrate p50/p95 and cost per token.
[05:00] Ajay (Lyra): our peak QPS estimate during open is ~120 requests/sec; average concurrency maybe 60. is 1 GPU enough?
[05:07] Priya (Redwood): 120 QPS for short 30-token responses likely needs multiple GPUs for headroom if you want low p95. the trial pool we'd propose is 2 GPUs with autoscale and burst to hosted. again we'll model in the worksheet.
[05:25] Rachel (Lyra): we want to compare three scenarios: fully hosted, hybrid hosted+dedicated, and private on-prem. can you list the gating factors for each?
[05:33] Liam (Redwood): sure — hosted: pros are fastest to ship and pay-as-you-go; cons: multi-tenant variability and less control over custom quant. dedicated: pros predictable throughput, cost savings at scale, private networking options; cons: monthly commitment and provisioning lead time. private: pros full isolation and compliance; cons: ops burden and higher baseline costs.
[05:56] Sofia (Lyra): do you have references or customers in finance with similar patterns?
[06:01] Liam (Redwood): yes, a few references — we'll share anonymized case studies and a benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:07] Ajay (Lyra): on instrumentation—how do we measure token-level cost in your console? we need per-route cost and token breakdown.
[06:16] Priya (Redwood): Console gives token-level cost, per-route latency, and trace hooks. you can export and tie to your billing. we also surface batching stats and cache hit rates so you can see real unit reductions.
[06:30] Rachel (Lyra): perfect. any gotchas we should be aware of when we run the trial?
[06:34] Priya (Redwood): things to watch: cold-starts for long-context requests, prompt engineering to maximize cache hits, and balancing batch window vs latency. also test mixed workloads — batch plus realtime can interact on the pool if not isolated.
[06:51] Sofia (Lyra): hmm. prompt engineering to maximize cache—do you have examples?
[06:55] Priya (Redwood): yes, keep stable system prompts, avoid sending large unrelated metadata every request; canonicalize user messages where possible. we'll include prompt tips in the follow-up deck.
[07:07] Rachel (Lyra): on pricing—do you charge for cache hits? like if KV cache returns keys, do we still get billed per token?
[07:13] Liam (Redwood): good nuance — billing is per generated token and per-embedding where applicable. cache hits that avoid regeneration reduce billed tokens; there may be a small fixed request charge depending on plan, but the major cost is generated tokens. we'll call out request vs token billing in the worksheet.
[07:31] Ajay (Lyra): what about egress costs for private? we host models in our VPC, so network egress isn't the same as hosted
[07:38] Liam (Redwood): for private, egress is under your infra. for dedicated hosted, data plane egress may apply depending on region. we'll include region-specific notes.
[07:47] Sofia (Lyra): curious about monitoring — can we set alerts on cost thresholds?
[07:52] Priya (Redwood): yes, console supports spend alerts, token burn alerts, and per-route budget constraints. you can auto-fallback to cheaper model or rate-limit when budget is hit.
[08:03] Rachel (Lyra): are there limits to batching that would affect p95? like maximum batch size?
[08:09] Priya (Redwood): batch size is configurable; larger batches help amortize kernel overhead but increase per-request wait. we usually pick dynamic batch windows and a max batch size tuned to latency SLOs.
[08:22] Ajay (Lyra): for our nightly summarization, we can tolerate higher latency. could we run that on a quantized model to save cost?
[08:29] Priya (Redwood): yes — batch jobs are prime candidates for aggressive quantization. we have curated quantized variants in hosted and more aggressive in dedicated/private. we'll recommend a model split in the worksheet.
[08:42] Rachel (Lyra): what about billing granularity — hourly, per-minute?
[08:46] Liam (Redwood): hosted is per token. dedicated has monthly reserved cost plus metered overages; we provide amortized per-token calculations for reserved pools in the worksheet.
[08:57] Sofia (Lyra): ok, let's talk timeline — we want a trial and decision in two weeks. is that realistic?
[09:03] Liam (Redwood): two weeks is tight but doable for a small dedicated trial if we get traffic profile today and sign the trial terms; otherwise we can start with hosted benchmark immediately.
[09:14] Ajay (Lyra): I'll share traffic stats and token mix by EOD tomorrow.
[09:18] Rachel (Lyra): and we'll need the SOC2 and security packet before the trial.
[09:22] Liam (Redwood): we'll attach both to the follow-up email.
[09:26] Priya (Redwood): quick note — we'll also propose a hybrid routing policy so you can route mission-critical chat to dedicated and less-critical to hosted to minimize cost during spikes.
[09:38] Sofia (Lyra): any examples of % cost split people use? like what percent dedicated vs hosted?
[09:44] Priya (Redwood): often customers put 60-80% of steady-state volume on dedicated and 20-40% on hosted for burst and fallback. depends on risk appetite.
[09:55] Rachel (Lyra): ok good. can Redwood share a sample benchmark script or CSV format for our load replay?
[10:01] Priya (Redwood): yes, we'll send a template and the benchmark plan.
[10:06] Liam (Redwood): recap — we'll send pricing worksheet, SOC2/security packet, benchmark plan and template, and propose trial sizing. next call: performance deep-dive (Priya-led) to run the benchmarks.
[10:20] Ajay (Lyra): sounds good. any other questions from our side?
[10:24] Sofia (Lyra): none from me.
[10:26] Rachel (Lyra): no. thanks.
[10:28] Liam (Redwood): thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the deep-dive.

[44:30] End call.

Notes / Artifacts referenced: Pricing worksheet (link), SOC2 + security packet (link: redwood.com/soc2.pdf), benchmark spreadsheet and replay template (link).
